title: The Monks' Meal Reflection
hookLine: dinner eaten over a phone, and the reflection monks make before the first bite
carry: the meal reflection: food to sustain, not for show
tomorrow: a king huffing after dinner. what did the Buddha tell him?

lines: NOT FOR FUN, PRIDE OR LOOKS.
ONLY TO KEEP THIS BODY GOING.
cards: A plate gets cleared without anyone tasting much of it. Eyes on a show, a thumb on a screen, and the food just disappears.

Before the first bite, monks in the Theravada tradition stop for a reflection, and the words are old: a monk uses his food wisely, the suttas say, not for fun, not for pride, not for looks, not to show off.
Only to keep this body going. It sounds strict, maybe even a little joyless, the kind of thing you'd skip. Taste it slowly, though, and it turns out to be about care.

teach.b: The reflection is in the Majjhima Nikaya, in a list of ways to keep the mind clear, and later teachers, like Buddhaghosa in the Path of Purification, explain it line by line.
The food is for the body's upkeep, to ease the discomfort of hunger, and to support the holy life.
Then a quiet promise: I'll end the old feeling of hunger and not stir up a new one from eating too much, and I'll live blameless and at ease. Notice what's missing. There's no rule against taste.
There's no claim that the body is bad.
The list just asks why the spoon is moving. For fun, for show, out of boredom, or to keep this body able to live and practice? That one question changes how a meal feels.
Here's a detail to pass on tonight: the reflection compares eating, in one telling, to putting medicine on a wound, so that it heals.

teach.h: NOT A FEAST, NOT A FAST.
teach.b: You don't put on more than the wound needs, and you don't skip it either.
Food with care sits between two mistakes: feasting without noticing, and refusing what the body needs. The Buddha himself, the tradition says, gave up harsh fasting before his awakening and ate.
Care for the body is part of the path, not a break from it.

how: In Theravada monasteries, monks and nuns recite a reflection on the proper use of food before eating; some lay Buddhists say it at home or pause in silence before a meal.

o: eating only plain food with no taste at all
saying a long blessing over every single dish
eating to keep the body well, knowing why you eat

games.q: the meal reflection — tap the pairs.

s: the meal reflection says taste is wrong
there's no rule against taste; it asks why you're eating.
the reflection compares eating to medicine on a wound
enough to heal, no more, and not skipped either.
mindful eating means eating as little as possible
food with care sits between feasting and refusing what the body needs.

games.q: you've had a hard day and want a second dessert to feel better. what does the meal reflection ask first?
o: nothing; desserts are never allowed on the path.
why is the spoon moving: hunger, or comfort and boredom?
eat it fast so you don't have to think about it.
games.why: the reflection doesn't ban food; it asks what the eating is for, the body's upkeep or something else.

practice: If you have anything to eat or drink nearby, a sip of tea, a raisin, a piece of bread, hold it first and smell it. Put it in your mouth and let it sit a moment before you chew.
Taste it all the way through, and notice the moment the body has had enough. Swallow, and pause before anything else.

wordCard.voice: Food with care: eating to keep this body going, tasting it, and knowing why the spoon is moving.

orig.note: Pali: patisankha yoniso, 'reflecting wisely', how the meal reflection begins.

carryVoice: Something for the next meal: the meal reflection, food to keep this body going, not for show, like medicine on a wound. Seven of nine.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 2 (Sabbasava Sutta: reflecting wisely, one uses almsfood not for amusement, intoxication, beautification or adornment, but for the body's endurance, to end discomfort, to support the holy life; ending old feelings, not arousing new ones)
Visuddhimagga I (the reflection on requisites explained; eating compared to dressing a wound)
Majjhima Nikaya 36 (the Bodhisatta gives up extreme fasting and takes solid food)
